title: Provider-side invoice-to-SOR validation for housing repairs

problem_severity_frequency.rationale: Primary council audit evidence that the control fails (Winchester CAB3557(H) 2026-07-06: backlog and delay authorising invoices, no cost breakdown on large work orders, 25 properties with duplication indications) plus a quantified overcharge (Brighton & Hove: ~GBP 300,000 from five SOR codes charged for materials not fitted) and a provider's own policy mandating the manual check (NLM 2026-03). The problem is frequent (every invoice), recurring and evidenced for this buyer. Scored 4 rather than 5 because the evidence is from a small number of councils and the sector-wide rate (SHAC 63%/66%) is weak secondary evidence. The persistence thesis is weak but supported, so the missing-why-now cap does not apply.

buyer_budget_clarity.rationale: The buyer is identified (repairs and maintenance finance function; Head of Landlord Services / Repairs and Maintenance Manager named in Winchester CAB3557(H); Finance Officer and Head of Assets named in NLM's policy) and there is evidence the buyer already pays for comparable work: salaried reconciliation roles at GBP 29,400-38,115 (St Mungo's, Onward Homes, Houghton Group) and Mears paying for an additional quantity-surveying resource. Scored 3 (adequate, evidenced for this buyer) rather than 4 because the spend is on headcount, not on a comparable software purchase, so the budget line for a product is inferred rather than demonstrated.

evidence_strength.rationale: Credible secondary and primary evidence about this buyer and market with no fatal desk objection: two council audit reports, a provider policy document, employer job advertisements, and a live competitor product. Scored 3 rather than 4 because the evidence is concentrated in a small number of providers and no buyer has been shown to purchase a comparable product.

distribution.rationale: Channels are plausible (internal-audit partnerships, CIH/NHF networks, repairs-manager community, contractors) but no prospect has been produced and the sector's procurement is framework-bound and slow. Capped at 2 under the 'plausible channel list' rule.

differentiation.rationale: Raised from 2 to 3 after the desk scan found no housing-management vendor occupying the provider-side invoice-to-SOR validation seam. The wedge is evidenced for this buyer and market (the check is unoccupied and the buyer already pays for the work), but it is not strong: Rentari.ai has already productised the mechanism in the US, and MYRO/Aareon/Ingentive are positioned to add it as a feature. Scored 3 (adequate, evidenced) rather than 4 because the evidence is a negative desk finding plus a documented feature-absorption risk.

validation_speed_cost.rationale: A decisive desk-only test exists (scan housing-management vendor roadmaps and release notes for a shipped or announced invoice-to-SOR validation feature) at GBP 0 and a few hours, with a pre-fixed stop rule. A follow-on interview test would be cheap but requires owner approval.

feasibility.rationale: Buildable with current document/LLM tooling (Rentari.ai proves the mechanism). Capped at 3 because the works-order integration is bespoke per provider and the NHF rate book is licensed to the provider, not the vendor, so the collection/integration steps are unproven.

economics.rationale: Modelled only, with no tested input. Price hypothesis GBP 500-2,000/month per provider or GBP 0.50-2.00 per invoice, anchored on the salaried role it replaces and the outsourced-bookkeeping per-transaction benchmark. Capped at 2 with low confidence under the untested-economics rule.

founder_fit.rationale: No evidence about the founder's access to UK social-housing finance teams or ability to do the work. Null until real evidence exists.

risk.rationale: No veto-level exposure: the product reads invoices the provider already holds and validates against a rate book the provider already licenses. Risks are commercial (feature absorption by suite vendors, slow framework procurement) rather than legal, privacy or platform. Scored 3.

economic_buyer.note: The buyer is identified and named in primary documents: the repairs and maintenance finance function, with the Head of Landlord Services / Repairs and Maintenance Manager owning the audit action plan (Winchester CAB3557(H)) and the Finance Officer / Head of Assets performing and authorising the check (NLM policy).

painful_frequent_or_budgeted.note: The problem is frequent (every contractor invoice, monthly) and budgeted: providers pay GBP 29,400-38,115/year for reconciliation staff, and Mears paid for an additional quantity-surveying resource after a GBP 300,000 overcharge. Council audits document the control failing.

non_paid_distribution.note: Channels are plausible (internal-audit partnerships, CIH/NHF networks, repairs-manager community, contractors) but no prospect has been produced and the sector's procurement is framework-bound.
non_paid_distribution.resolve_via: Identify one non-paid channel that produces a conversation with a repairs finance manager, without paid acquisition.

defensible_wedge.note: Desk scan (2026-09-22) found no housing-management vendor that has shipped or announced invoice-to-SOR validation: MYRO tracks the lifecycle to invoice closure and reports contractor cost but does not validate lines against the rate book; Fixflo applies SOR to works-order costing; Oneserve, Aareon, SDM, CHICS and MRI Greentree have no such feature; Dwellant's S20 warning is a total-level alarm; Plentific compares to the approved quote, not the rate book. The seam is unoccupied today, but the finding is a negative desk check rather than affirmative evidence of a durable wedge, and MYRO/Aareon/Ingentive are one release away from adding it.
defensible_wedge.resolve_via: Interview two or three repairs finance managers (owner approval required) to test whether the provider would buy a standalone check or wait for its suite vendor; if the answer is 'wait', this filter fails.

no_network_effects_needed.note: The check delivers value to a single provider on its own invoices; no network effects are required.

plausible_margins.note: Modelled only. Price hypothesis GBP 500-2,000/month per provider or GBP 0.50-2.00 per invoice; processing cost per invoice unknown; the works-order integration may be bespoke per customer, which would create a service burden.
plausible_margins.resolve_via: Model contribution margin against a realistic invoice volume and processing cost, and test whether the works-order integration can be standardised.

acceptable_risk.note: No veto-level legal, regulatory, privacy, trust or platform risk: the product reads invoices the provider already holds and validates against a rate book the provider already licenses. Commercial risk (feature absorption, slow procurement) is real but not veto-level.

cheap_disconfirming_test.note: A decisive desk-only test exists: scan housing-management vendor roadmaps and release notes for a shipped or announced invoice-to-SOR validation feature, at GBP 0 and a few hours, with a pre-fixed stop rule.

not_all_optimistic.note: Viability currently requires several optimistic assumptions to hold simultaneously: that a provider buys a standalone check rather than waiting for its suite vendor; that the works-order integration can be standardised; that the rate-book licence permits vendor consumption; and that the economics work at realistic pricing.
not_all_optimistic.resolve_via: Resolve the standalone-vs-feature question first (the desk scan); if the check is a feature, the idea fails regardless of the other assumptions.
